name: Accused of Domestic Violence: What Happens Next?

step.name: Step 1: The Initial Report and Arrest. Domestic violence cases often begin with a 911 call, after which law enforcement responds. Officers investigate on-site and, if they determine probable cause exists, they'll make an arrest. This typically happens very quickly, and you might be taken into custody even if you believe the accusation is unfounded. This phase can take a few hours to a day, leading to booking and potentially bail being set.

Officers investigate on-site and, if they determine probable cause exists, they'll make an arrest. This typically happens very quickly, and you might be taken into custody even if you believe the accusation is unfounded. step.name: Step 2: Arraignment and Protective Order Issuance. After arrest, you'll be brought before a judge for an arraignment, usually within a few days. Here, the charges will be formally read, and you'll enter a plea. A judge will almost always issue a temporary criminal protective order (CPO) at this stage, which can prevent you from contacting the alleged victim and returning to your home. This order can significantly disrupt your life immediately.

step.name: Step 3: Pre-Trial Hearings and Discovery. The period following arraignment involves several court dates, known as pre-trial hearings, which can stretch over weeks or months. During this time, your attorney will receive discovery (evidence from the prosecution), investigate the allegations, interview witnesses, and file motions to challenge the evidence. Negotiations with the prosecutor for a plea agreement often occur during this phase, with the aim of reducing charges or finding alternative resolutions.

step.name: Step 4: Evidentiary Hearings and Trial. If a plea agreement isn't reached, the case will proceed to evidentiary hearings and potentially a trial. At trial, both sides present their evidence, and a judge or jury decides your guilt or innocence. Domestic violence trials can be emotionally charged and legally complex, requiring skilled courtroom advocacy. This can be a lengthy process, often several months, depending on court schedules and case complexity.

step.name: Step 5: Sentencing (if convicted). If you are convicted, or if you accept a plea bargain, a sentencing hearing will follow. The judge will consider factors like the severity of the offense, your criminal history, and any mitigating circumstances to determine the appropriate penalties. These can range from probation and anger management classes to significant jail time. Navigating these steps requires dedicated legal expertise, which Angelo J. Reyes, APC offers to clients across San Diego County.
